text:
So is this a bubble?

The European Central Bank's economists think a correction is likely, and that euro area households would feel it mostly through their funds.

In September we got a preview. The Nasdaq one hundred lost more than six hundred billion dollars in two days.

Within a week, it had bounced back by trillions. Fear, then greed, then fear again.

Let's put today next to the year 2000.

The top ten companies in the S and P five hundred: about twenty-six percent of the index then. Close to forty now.

Valuations: forty-four times ten-year earnings at the peak. Around forty-one now.

And the US share of the world index: roughly half back then, more than seventy percent today.

On paper, today is just as stretched, and more concentrated.

There is one big difference. Today's giants are enormously profitable. In 2000, many internet darlings had no earnings at all.

But profitable doesn't mean cheap. Cisco was very profitable in 2000. Its share price still fell by more than eighty percent.

And bubbles can run much longer than anyone expects. In December 1996, Alan Greenspan warned about irrational exuberance. The Nasdaq then almost quadrupled before it crashed.

So nobody knows when, or if, this ends. What we can do is look at what happened to Europeans the last times it did.

We've been here twice before.

December 1989. Japan is the hottest stock market on Earth, and at its peak it makes up around forty-two percent of the entire global stock market.

Japanese stocks traded at around sixty times earnings. If you bought the world in 1989, you mostly bought Japan.

The Nikkei closed that year at almost thirty-nine thousand points. It took thirty-four years, until February 2024, to see that level again.

Today Japan is around six percent of the world index.

But here's the part almost nobody tells you. A world index investor in 1989 was not ruined.

As Japan shrank, the index automatically shifted to everything else. In dollars, the world index was back to its 1989 level within about four years.

That's the self-cleaning feature of a market cap index. It concentrates into bubbles, but it also lets the losers shrink.

The second time was March 2000. For a moment, Cisco, a company that makes network equipment, was the most valuable company in the world.

Then it broke. The Nasdaq one hundred fell more than eighty percent, and needed more than fifteen years to get back to its peak.

Europe was not a safe place to hide. The Euro Stoxx fifty lost about two thirds of its value from 2000 to 2003.

In Germany, Deutsche Telekom was sold to ordinary families as the people's share. It traded above one hundred euros in March 2000, and below ten two years later.

Millions of first-time investors lost around ninety percent, and a whole generation of Germans swore off the stock market.

It's worth looking at how that crash actually unfolded, because it didn't feel like a crash at the start.

In euros, world stocks lost six percent in 2000. Then twelve percent in 2001. Then thirty-three percent in 2002.

A slow bleed for two years, and the worst year last. Each time it looked like the bottom, and each time it wasn't.

Compare that with 2008, one brutal year of minus thirty-seven, or 2022, minus thirteen. Bubbles tend to deflate slowly, which is exactly what wears people down.

And in 2000 the E C B was raising rates, to four point seven five percent by October. Today it's raising again, to two point five. Not the same level, but the same direction.
